'''Georg von Peuerbach''' (also '''Purbach''', '''Peurbach'''; {{langx|la|Purbachius}}; 30 May 1423 – 8 April 1461<ref name=":3">{{NDB|20|281|282|Peu(e)rbach (auch Purbach), Georg von (eigentlich Georg Aunpekh)|Hermann Haupt|118790684}}</ref>) was an [[Austria]]n [[astronomer]], [[poet]], [[mathematician]] and [[Scientific instrument|instrument]] maker, best known for his streamlined presentation of [[Ptolemaic astronomy]] in the ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum.'' Peuerbach was instrumental in making astronomy, mathematics and literature simple and accessible for Europeans during the [[Renaissance]] and beyond.

==Biography==
Peuerbach's life remains relatively unknown until he enrolled at the [[University of Vienna]] in 1446.<ref name="Britannica2">{{cite web|last=Shank|first=Michael|title=Georg von Peuerbach|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/454669/Georg-von-Peuerbach|access-date=2014-03-09|publisher=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]}}</ref> He was born in the Austrian town of [[Peuerbach]] in upper Austria. A horoscope published eighty-nine years after his death places his date of birth specifically on 30 May 1423, though other evidence only indicates that he was born sometime after 1421'''.'''<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=J.|first=Aiton, E.|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/427988275|title=Peurbach's Theoricae novae planetarum, a translation with commentary|date=1987|publisher=Dept. of History and Sociology of Science, University of Pennsylvania|isbn=0-934235-08-2|oclc=427988275}}</ref> He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1448.

Peuerbach's intellect was discovered by a priest of his hometown, Dr. Heinrich Barucher. Dr. Barucher recognized Peuerbach's academic abilities from a young age and put him in contact with the Augustinian provost of [[Klosterneuburg Monastery]], Georg Muestinger.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Horst |first=Thomas |date=2019 |title=The Reception of Cosmography in Vienna: Georg von Peuerbach, Johannes Regiomontanus, and Sebastian Binderlius |url=https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3039807_7/component/file_3058064/content |journal=Max Planck Institute for the History of Science}}</ref> Georg Muestinger taught a course at the University of Vienna entitled ''Theoricae Planetarum.'' These lectures were the first that Georg von Peuerbach attended at the University of Vienna and inspired him to enroll.

During his time at University of Vienna, Peuerbach received a master of philosophy in 1446 and a second master's degree in 1448, studying mathematics under the guidelines of [[Johannes von Gmunden|Johann von Gmünden]].<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1007/978-0-387-30400-7_1081 | chapter=Peurbach &#91;Peuerbach, Purbach&#93;, Georg von | title=The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers | date=2007 | last1=Green | first1=Daniel W. E. | pages=897–898 | isbn=978-0-387-31022-0 }}</ref> His curriculum was composed primarily of humanities courses, as was usual at the time.<ref name="O'Connor2">{{cite web |author=J. J. O'Connor |author2=E. F. Robertson |title=Georg Peuerbach |url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Peurbach.html |access-date=2014-03-09}}</ref> His knowledge of astronomy derived from independent study, possibly from studying under followers of John von Gmünden.<ref name=":1" /> During his enrollment, there were no professors of astronomy at the University of Vienna.<ref name="O'Connor2" /> However, under his tutelage astronomic studies emerged at the University of Vienna throughout the 15th and 16th centuries.

Peuerbach observed the [[occultation]] of [[Jupiter]] by the Moon in 1451, signifying the beginning of his personal astronomy career. After this point Peuerbach essentially devoted his life to astronomy, developing tools and theories, and collaborating with his pupil [[Regiomontanus]] (Johannes Müller von Königsberg) to make astrology more digestible to common people.<ref>{{Citation |last=Green |first=Daniel W. E. |title=Peurbach &#91;Peuerbach, Purbach&#93;, Georg von |date=2007 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-30400-7_1081 |encyclopedia=The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers |pages=897–898 |editor-last=Hockey |editor-first=Thomas |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-30400-7_1081 |isbn=978-0-387-30400-7 |access-date=2021-11-04 |editor2-last=Trimble |editor2-first=Virginia |editor3-last=Williams |editor3-first=Thomas R. |editor4-last=Bracher |editor4-first=Katherine|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Majority of Georg's astrological discoveries were made in the last ten years of his life.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aiton |first=E. J. |date=January 1987 |title=Peurbach's Theoricae Novae Planetarum: A Translation with Commentary |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1086/368660 |journal=Osiris |volume=3 |pages=4–43 |doi=10.1086/368660 |s2cid=144525057 |issn=0369-7827|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Georg Peuerbach traveled through central and southern Europe, most notably in [[Italy]], giving lectures on astronomy. His lectures led to offers of professorships at several universities, including those at [[Bologna]] and [[Padua]]. During this time he also met Italian astronomer [[Giovanni Bianchini]] of [[Ferrara]], perhaps the leading astronomer at the time, and the Cardinal [[Nicholas of Cusa]].<ref name="O'Connor2" /> He returned to the University of Vienna in 1453, earned his Masters of Arts, and began lecturing on Latin poetry.<ref name="Britannica2" /> He is often credited as a leader in reviving classical Greek and Roman literature in arts and sciences.<ref name=":1" />

Peuerbach attended many university lectures that focused on Roman poets, which led to him playing one of the leading roles in the revitalization of classical learning introduced by [[Pope Pius II|Aenaes Silvius Piccolomini]].<ref name=":1" /> Peuerbach eventually followed the advice of the court astrologer to [[Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor|Emperor Friedrich III]] in [[Wiener Neustadt|Wiener-Nestadt]], Johann Nihil, and took the position of court astrologer to the king of [[Hungary]]. After being court astrologer for a few years, Peuerbach eventually went on to become imperial [[An Astrologer|astrologer]].<ref name=":1" />

While at Vienna in 1454, Peuerbach taught planetary motion to students at the university. Peuerbach's lectures were based on Ptolemaic teachings and became so famous that from 1472 they were printed under the title ‘''Theoricae Novae Planetarum''‘.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Tietz |first=Tabea |date=2020-05-30 |title=Georg von Peuerbach – Astronomy at the Beginning of the Scientific Revolution in Early Modern Age |url=http://scihi.org/georg-von-peuerbach/ |access-date=2022-12-04 |website=SciHi Blog |language=en-US}}</ref> 

In 1454 Peuerbach was appointed court [[astrologer]] to King [[Ladislas V]] of Bohemia and Hungary. It was in this capacity that Peuerbach first met Ladislas' cousin Frederick who was then serving as guardian to the 14-year-old king and who would later become [[Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor]]. Ladislas resided primarily in [[Prague]] and Vienna, allowing Peuerbach to maintain his position at the University of Vienna. During this time Peuerbach met Regiomontanus, who was then a student at the university. After Regiomontanus graduated in 1452 at the age of 15, he began collaborating extensively with Peuerbach in his astronomical work.<ref name="O'Connor2" />
In 1457, following the assassination of two notable political figures, Ladislas fled Vienna and died in 1458. Peurbach did not receive an appointment from either of Ladislas' two successors.<ref name="O'Connor2" /> However he was asked to be the ''Astronomus caesaris'' for Emperor [[Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor|Frederick III]], which is the position he held until his death.<ref name=":2" />

Georg von Peuerbach died on 8 April 1461. His work set the path for future scholars, scientists, and astronomers for years to come; Peurbach’s early death was a serious loss to the progress of astronomy,<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Georg Peurbach - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Peurbach/ |access-date=2022-12-04 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> although [[Regiomontanus]], his successor, was able to continue his work.   

==Work==
[[File:Tractatus Georgi Peurbachii super propositiones Ptolemaei de sinubus & chordis.agr.jpg|thumb|Page from Peurbach's sine table]]

Peuerbach is best-known for his work ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum,'' written in 1454, and published by his disciple Regiomontanus in 1472.<ref name=":02">[https://www.cairn-int.info/abstract-E_RHS_652_0339--the-early-manuscripts-of-georg-von.htm# "The Early Manuscripts of Georg von Peuerbach's Theoricae Novae Planetarum"]</ref> ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum'' presented a version of [[Ptolemy|Claudius Ptolemy]] geocentric system in a more colloquial and comprehensible way.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dekker |first=Elly |title=The Collection of Orbs, Spheres and Globes in Florence |date=2005 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23993598 |journal=Globe Studies |issue=51/52 |pages=85–102 |jstor=23993598 |issn=1684-7091}}</ref> Based on a series of Peuerbach's lectures at [[:de:Bürgerschule|Bürgerschule]] in Vienna that were transcribed by Regiomontanus.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nothaft |first=Philipp |date=February 2019 |title=An Alfonsine universe: Nicolò Conti and Georg Peurbach on the threefold motion of the fixed stars. |url= https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:84856a94-c62b-4199-8700-fa5d481753a4|journal=Centaurus |volume=61 |issue=1/2 |pages=91–110 |doi=10.1111/1600-0498.12200 |s2cid=182722802 |via=EBSCO}}</ref> The book introduced the "New Planetary Theory of Georg von Peuerbach" based on the already successful Ptolemaic system, this new theory presented the physical realities of eccentric planetary spheres.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zotti |first=Georg |date=2019-04-23 |title="Harmony and Symmetry". European Society for Astronomy in Culture (SEAC) 26, Graz 27th August–1st September 2018 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1558/jsa.38829 |journal=Journal of Skyscape Archaeology |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=95–98 |doi=10.1558/jsa.38829 |s2cid=201890819 |issn=2055-348X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In his model of the sun Peuerbach removed simple eccentric shells and added partial orbs, some of which were eccentric and some concentric to the center of the world. Similar models for the planets replaced the body of the sun with an epicycle sphere carrying each planet.

Peuerbach's ideas replaced ''Theorica Planetarum Communis'', a work credited to [[Gerard of Cremona|Gerardus Cremonensis]], as the standard university text on astronomy and was studied by many influential astronomers including [[Nicolaus Copernicus]] and [[Johannes Kepler]].<ref name="Britannica2" />

In 1457 Peuerbach observed an eclipse and noted that it had occurred 8 minutes earlier than had been predicted by the [[Alfonsine tables|Alphonsine Tables]], the best available astronomical tables at the time. He then computed his own set of eclipse tables, the ''Tabulae Eclipsium.'' Widely read in manuscript form beginning around 1459 and formally published in 1514, these tables remained highly influential for many years.<ref name="Britannica2" /><ref name="O'Connor2" />

Peuerbach wrote various papers on practical mathematics and constructed various [[astronomical instrument]]s. Most notably, he computed [[sine tables]] based on techniques developed by Islamicate mathematicians.<ref name="Britannica2" /> Peuerbach's work was instrumental in establishing a more modern understanding of mathematics.

In 1460, [[Basilios Bessarion|Cardinal Johannes Bessarion]], while visiting Frederick's court seeking assistance in a crusade to reclaim [[Constantinople]] from the Turks, proposed that Peuerbach and Regiomontanus create a new translation of [[Ptolemy]]'s ''[[Almagest]]'' from the original Greek. Bessarion thought that a shorter and more clearly written version of the work would make a suitable teaching text. Peuerbach accepted the task and worked on it with Regiomontanus until his death in 1461, at which time 6 volumes had been completed. Regiomontanus completed the project, and the final version containing 13 volumes was published in 1496.<ref name="O'Connor2" />

== Accomplishments ==

* In February 1453, Georg Von Peuerbach was awarded with the [[Magister artium|Magister Artium]] in Vienna.<ref name=":2" />
* Peuerbach began the translation of [[Almagest|Ptolemy's Almagest]] from Greek into Latin, a task which was completed and published by his student [[Regiomontanus]] in 1496.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mathematical Treasure: Peuerbach's and Regiomontanus's Ptolemy {{!}} Mathematical Association of America |url=https://www.maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/mathematical-treasure-peuerbach-s-and-regiomontanus-s-ptolemy |access-date=2022-12-06 |website=www.maa.org}}</ref>
* Expanded the Astronomy program at the University of Vienna.
* Influenced many other European astrological and astronomical discoveries with his observations and ideologies

== Legacy ==
Georg von Peuerbach's work outlives him because of his ability to communicate astronomy, mathematics and art. His contributions simplified seeming difficult ideas, making them more digestible and inspiring critical thought. Through his tutelage he was able to create an astronomy program at his alma mater, further expanding the understanding of astronomy.

Peuerbach's and [[Regiomontanus]]'s contribution expanded the European understanding of astronomy by translating Ptolemy's ''Almagest'' in a book that later influenced [[Nicolaus Copernicus]].<ref name="Britannica2" /> Though the work was completed after Peuerbach's death in 1461, Regiomontanus carried on with the task and eventually the ''Epitome of the Almagest'' was published in 1496, nearly 35 years after his teacher’s death, and 20 years after his own (Regiomontanus died in 1476).<ref name=":1" /> This book would go on to be an important reference for Nicholas Copernicus for the creation of his book ''De Revolutionibus''.<ref name="Britannica2" />

Ironically Nicolaus Copernicus's work, and later [[Isaac Newton|Sir Issac Newton's]], disproved many of the ideas that Peuerbach supported while defending the Ptolemaic system, nonetheless his advancement in technology and theory help modernize the study of astronomy.

Peuerbach's input in Regiomontanus's trigonometric tables was used by future astronomers in the coming century.<ref name=":1" />  Though a fair amount of Peuerbach's work is believed to have circulated in academia, his full observations were only published by Johann Schöner nearly a century after Peuerbach's death.<ref name="Britannica2" /> His ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum'' would be released in numerous editions between 1472 and 1596, with additions by scholars such as Regiomontanus, Peter Apian, [[Erasmus Reinhold]], and [[Philip Melanchthon]]. It is believed that by 1653, at least 56 Latin printings of the text had been published with numerous editions in other languages as well.<ref name=":1" />

Peuerbach’s ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum'' became one of the most common astronomy textbooks used to train future scholars.<ref name=":1" /> He is credited with being instrumental in the European understanding of astronomy and the Ptolemaic system. The descriptions of the solid spheres model (common to the Ptolemaic planetary system) seen in the ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum'' would remain the accepted view of the nature of the spheres until the time of [[Tycho Brahe]], who disproved the existence of solid spheres.<ref name=":1" /> The ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum'' is also credited with helping to establish much of the technical vocabulary used by astronomers through the seventeenth century.<ref name=":1" />

Peuerbach is also known to have developed and distributed tables that were capable of predicting eclipses of both the sun and the moon, and this practice was continued by Regiomontanus.<ref name="Britannica2" /> The manuscript, titled ''Tabulae Eclipsium'', saw continued use, as late as Tycho Brahe near the end of the sixteenth century.  He is also believed to have overseen the collection and duplication of numerous astronomical manuscripts.<ref name="Britannica2" /> This culminated in the development of a scientific printing press in [[Nuremberg]] by Regiomontanus. The printing press was further used to publish astronomical works such as Peuerbach's own ''Theoricae Novae Planetarum'', as well as the ''Astronomicon'' written by the poet Manilius<ref name="Britannica2" />
